title: Drive a hand impact driver with a hammer: hold its bit seated and square in a seized rotor screw, then strike the cap
instruction: Break the seized rotor screw loose with the impact driver and the hammer, then put both tools down off the hub and let go of them.
context: Rotor changes are a frequent shop job on Honda Civics, Accords and CR-Vs, among the best-selling cars in the US, and on many other Japanese cars, where the rotor is held to the hub by two countersunk Phillips screws that after a few winters are almost always rusted in. Automotive service technicians and mechanics hold 825,800 US jobs (BLS, 2025). Rotors are usually changed on the car; here the hub and knuckle are on the bench, as in a wheel-bearing job, the less common case. A screwdriver only cams out and strips the recess, and the screw then has to be drilled out. The shop tool is the hand impact driver: the technician seats the bit fully, holds the driver square with one hand and strikes its cap with a hammer in the other; a helical cam inside turns the bit while the blow forces it into the recess. A blow on a bit not fully home, or a driver held off square, cams it out and chews the recess.
setup: Positions in metres from the midpoint between the two arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left; heights above the table top. A car's front hub and knuckle, off the car, stand hub-up on a bench stand (a 16 x 16 cm, 12 mm steel foot plate and a 70 mm post), the hub's axis at (0.40, -0.06). Rotor: a cast-iron 262 mm front rotor, its 22 mm friction ring from 6.0 to 8.2 cm up, its 150 mm hat rising to its face 10.5 cm up (6 mm face, rusted). Through the rotor's centre bore: the hub's 56 mm pilot, 6 mm proud; four M12 x 1.5 wheel studs on a 100 mm circle at 45, 135, 225 and 315 degrees, standing 38 mm proud. The rotor is held to the hub by two M6 x 1.0 countersunk Phillips screws on a 40 mm radius: the one at (0.40, -0.10) is already out (its 14 mm square opening in the hat's face is empty); the other (ISO 7046, 12 mm head, PH3 recess 6.6 mm across and 3.6 mm deep), at (0.40, -0.02), is in, its head flush with the hat's face, and seized: no torque a hand can put through a driver turns it. A hand impact driver (3/8 in drive, 0.65 kg; black-oxide knurled body 36 mm across and 105 mm long, chrome striking cap 39 mm across, 22 mm nose, PH3 impact bit; 170 mm from bit tip to cap; the body slides 3 mm down over the anvil against a 20 N return spring, and its cam turns the bit 12 degrees over that stroke) stands nose-down in a hardwood block (80 x 80 x 70 mm with a 30 mm square pocket 55 mm deep) at (0.46, -0.29), its body resting on the block. A 16 oz ball-peen hammer (forged steel head 100 mm long with a 29 mm face, 0.45 kg; 323 mm hickory handle, 22 x 30 mm; 0.62 kg in all) stands on its face on a stepped hardwood stand at (0.40, 0.125) (lower step 70 x 150 mm, 100 mm tall, under the head; upper step 70 x 90 mm, 45 mm higher, under the handle from 30 to 120 mm from the head's axis), its handle along +y resting on the upper step and running to y = 0.46. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: Watched every control step (20 Hz), and every physics step (240 Hz) for the blows, in the hub's frame. A blow is a PhysX contact between the hammer and the driver's body passing an impulse of at least 0.2 N s in one physics step, after the hammer's face has been at least 5 cm off the cap. It counts only on a held driver (a gripper within 5 mm of the driver's body at the last control step; otherwise nothing), and only if the face's centre is over the 39 mm cap (within 19.5 mm of the driver's axis; an estimate of where a blow stops driving the cap squarely) and the face within 20 degrees of square (otherwise: glancing, no effect), and the face closed on the cap at 1.8 m/s or more (about 0.7 J in the 0.45 kg head: a firm deliberate blow but under half a mechanic's, 2 to 6 J at 3 to 5 m/s; the turn is not tied to the blow's energy, so 12 degrees per blow is generous) over the last physics steps before the contact (otherwise: a tap, no effect). A blow with the bit's tip more than 8 mm from the screw (in the air, or in the empty hole) does nothing. A blow on the screw is a cam-out unless, just before it, the bit's tip was within 1.0 mm of its axis and at least 2.0 mm deep in its recess (fully home is 3.1 mm) and the driver's axis within 5 degrees of the screw's; after two cam-outs the screw is stripped (later blows do nothing). Otherwise the blow is good if it drives the driver's 3 mm stroke at least 2 mm deeper than it was just before the contact, within 50 ms (pressing the body down first and then tapping it does not count): the cam turns the bit and the screw 12 degrees counter-clockwise; if not, nothing. 0 if at any time a tool falls off the table (its centre more than 5 cm below the table top). Otherwise, at the end: 0.8 x min(degrees turned / 30, 1) less 0.1 per cam-out (0 if stripped, never below 0): 0.32 per good blow, 0.8 once loose (30 degrees: three good blows). Plus 0.2 once the screw is loose and unstripped, both tools are down off the hub (every part at least 5 mm from the hub, rotor, studs and screws), every part of both grippers is at least 2 cm from both tools, and both tools are still (under 1 cm/s). Without success the score is at most 0.9. 1.0 (success): the screw loose with no cam-out, the tools down off the hub, let go and still, held for 1 s. Doing nothing, or refusing, scores 0.
reset_notes: On a real hub, each trial needs a fresh seized screw in the left-hand hole (the right-hand hole stays empty): fit a new M6 x 1.0 x 12 countersunk Phillips screw with a drop of thread-locking compound (or rust it in with salt spray for a few days) and check that 6 N m on a screwdriver does not turn it. Put the driver back in its block and the hammer back on its stand. The screw breaks loose when it has turned 30 degrees: mark the head and the hat with a paint line and read the angle with a protractor; cam-outs show as a burred recess (inspect with a loupe).
fidelity: Rigid bodies, 240 Hz; all parts full size. Recess: an 8-sided cone (cross drawn, not colliding); bit tip: a stepped cone, so it seats but can't grip in torsion: the screw turns only by the cam. Driver: an articulation with the 3 mm sprung stroke; its cam is a drive set from the stroke each physics step. Blows: PhysX contact impulse, hammer speed, stroke. Seized screw: a stiff joint moved 12 degrees per good blow. Turn per blow and thresholds are estimates.
